title: Sunny Liang Tan
text:
I obtained my Bachelor’s degree in Economics and Finance from University of Hong Kong in 2019, and Master of Arts in Economics from Duke University in 2021. I was a visiting scholar at MIT Department of Economics from 2024-2025. Prior to academia, I worked as an analyst at Softbank Venture Capital.
I grew up in Hunan province in mainland China where we are known for our spicy-eating culture.

title: Research
text:
Using Chinese VAT administrative data and VC/PE records, I construct firm-level investment and transaction measures and apply a matched staggered difference-in-differences design to identify the causal effects of government industrial guidance funds on productive efficiency, capital allocation, labor demand, and sales growth, as well as upstream and downstream spillovers. The funds target innovative firms, whose expansion subsequently promotes growth and innovation among downstream firms. I further incorporate innovation into a Baqaee-Farhi production-network model and quantify the aggregate output gains from government venture capital investment. The results provide an economic rationale for industrial policy in the presence of induced learning along production networks.

title: Sunny Liang Tan
text:
Working Papers

Exchange-Rate Movements and U.S. Corporations (Expected October 2026)
*Joint with Ivo Welch and Yuqing Zhou
Use U.S. Census LFTTD microdata and shift-share instruments to estimate the effects of exchange-rate exposure and the associated elasticities for exports, sales, and equity returns. The study provides firm-level micro evidence showing that the apparent macro-level exchange rate-stock market disconnect does not hold.

title: Research
text:
Work in Progress





Are Banks Discriminatory? Evidence from U.S. Residential Lending





We merge court-order data with bank Call Reports to construct a matched panel of more than two million observations and use a difference-in-differences design to identify the causal effects of judicial interventions on lending behavior and bank credit-supply elasticity.





Sunny Liang Tan, Jon Vogel







Coordination in Production Networks





Using Chinese VAT administrative data, I study complementarities when upstream and downstream firms receive investment simultaneously. I examine how information frictions, financing constraints, and decentralized decision-making generate under-coordination, and whether government coordination and policy intervention can internalize production-network complementarities.
